title: TurboProm: Low Cost and High Performance Metrics Observability at Scale
summary:
Many large enterprise and cloud deployments rely on metrics observability solutions (e.g., Prometheus) to monitor key performance indicators of system health (e.g., CPU, memory, network, app-level statistics). Monitoring and analyzing these metrics presents a significant challenge in terms of cost-latency tradeoffs at scale. Ideally, system operators would like immediately deployable and backwards compatible solutions to improve the cost-latency tradeoffs without significant impact on the fidelity of their observability applications. Unfortunately, existing solutions including state-of-art timeseries databases and custom approximate querying solutions fail on one or more aspects.
  In this paper, we present the design and implementation of TurboProm, a backwards-compatible drop-in accelerator for metrics observability deployments. TurboProm recasts metrics analytics tasks using a semantic-preserving summary view rather than classical query-centric view. Instead of estimating query results on raw timeseries metrics data, TurboProm uses semantic-preserving summaries that enable high-fidelity analytics with significant cost-latency improvements. We present a practical implementation of TurboProm that can be retrofitted to any existing observability deployment. We evaluate TurboProm on diverse real and synthetic workloads against state-of-art solutions and show that it can provide significant reduction in query latency and cost. TurboProm is open-source at https://github.com/ProjectASAP/ASAPQuery.

title: Recall-Bounded Staleness for Filtered Multi-Tenant ANN Graph Indexes under Concurrent Updates
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 3 Pages supplemental Proof
summary: Production vector search must continuously ingest, delete, and re-tenant vectors while serving low-latency, high-recall, metadata-filtered approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) queries for many tenants with per-tenant service-level objectives. Existing graph-based ANN systems address these requirements largely in isolation, leaving recall during concurrent re-optimization without an analytical bound. We develop a graph-based index that combines streaming updates, filtered search, and multi-tenancy, with one theoretical result and two system mechanisms. Our theory decomposes per-tenant recall loss into staleness from updates not yet integrated into the graph and filtered navigability determined by the local density of points satisfying a tenant's predicate. The staleness component exhibits anti-amortization on a merge-based graph, integrating a larger batch of inserts increases recall degradation super-linearly, so larger merges do not reduce total staleness loss. Holding the insert horizon fixed while increasing merge size 20x, we observe a monotonic decrease in terminal recall@10 from 99.44% to 99.01%. For filtered search, the theory gives a parameter-free frontier-mass relationship in local predicate density and a query-averaged per-tenant recall bound. We instantiate the bound with a filter and tenant-aware staging cache and a select-not-resize scheduler with per-tenant staleness ceilings. On a FreshDiskANN substrate, the ceiling eliminates tight-tier SLA violations under the evaluated churn workload, while merge reordering changes terminal recall by only 0.02 percentage points. The results show how recall bounds can guide background maintenance without relying on merge resizing as a recall control mechanism.

title: Join Order Enumeration and Optimization for Double-Star and Helix Join Graphs
summary: Join ordering is classic problem in data management. We highlight the connection between structure-specific dynamic programming algorithms and the mathematical enumeration of the possible merge trees from a join graph. We present two case studies, on double-star and helix shaped join graphs, that we believe carry useful techniques for a toolbox of building structure-specific join optimizers. For the double-star case, we show how the enumeration leads directly to a significantly improved search algorithm, whereas for the helix case we show that a algorithm derived from the mathematical enumeration is not necessarily better than structure-agnostic algorithms.

title: The Case for Single-Version Concurrency Control in the Cloud
comment: Accepted to CIDR'27
summary: Multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) has been the dominant concurrency protocol in modern database management systems (DBMSs). However, cloud-native HTAP architectures shift many of MVCC's traditional advantages from the primary transaction engine to the deployment architecture. Now, transactional and analytical processing are decoupled into loosely synchronized engines, while cloud deployment primitives provide the workload isolation required for this design. In this paper, we challenge the status quo, arguing that single-version concurrency control (SVCC) is better suited to cloud transaction processing than MVCC. Through a systematic analysis of MVCC's limitations, we show that SVCC avoids these shortcomings through a more lightweight and efficient design. Beyond arguing for a lighter transaction processing, we use this SVCC effort as a blueprint to advocate for a broader rethinking of cloud-native architectures and to outline a research roadmap to shape next-generation DBMSs.

title: SemReuse: Certified Reuse of Cached Natural-Language Views for Semantic Operators
summary: Semantic operators allow users to filter unstructured data using conditions expressed in natural language, but existing systems typically invoke an LLM for every input tuple. Analytical workloads often contain repeated or related filters whose results could be reused. Such reuse is risky because it requires inferring whether filter conditions are equivalent, whether one implies another, or whether they are mutually exclusive. An incorrect judgment can omit qualifying tuples or include nonqualifying ones. We introduce SemReuse, a system for safely reusing previous semantic-filter results. SemReuse stores each result as a materialized view and compares new filters with existing views to identify tuples that can provisionally be accepted or skipped without another LLM call. Because these decisions rely on a fallible language reasoner, SemReuse audits every rewritten result. Its pooled stratified audit uses exact finite-population bounds to provide jointly valid per-query recall and precision guarantees. If the requested guarantees cannot be established, SemReuse evaluates additional tuples and progressively approaches full evaluation. Thus, incorrect relation judgments affect efficiency rather than the validity of the reported guarantees. Experiments on large labeled corpora and real LLM executions show reductions of up to 15.4x. They also identify cross-filter inconsistency as the main source of repair cost.

title: CellChain: Benchmarking Cross-Scale Evidence Use for Perturbation Reasoning
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures
summary: Recent advances in foundation models and large-scale cellular perturbation datasets have driven growing interest in using LLMs to predict and reason about cellular responses. Biological reasoning in this setting involves relating molecular mechanisms, cellular responses, and functional outcomes across scales. Evaluating foundation models therefore requires assessing not only whether their predictions are correct, but also how those predictions depend on the biological evidence provided. We introduce CellChain, an experimentally grounded benchmark comprising 590 biological cases and 2,360 matched evidence-condition instances across gene-dependency prediction, cytokine-axis identification, and drug-sensitivity ranking. CellChain links perturbation experiments and external biological resources through a provenance-aware evidence graph spanning molecular, pathway, transcriptional, and phenotypic information. Task-specific conditions vary evidence coverage, composition, or assignment while preserving questions, candidate answers, reference targets, and scoring rules. Across 18 foundation models, the highest accuracies under prespecified target-evidence conditions are 57.5%, 75.5%, and 70.8%, respectively, and broader evidence coverage does not consistently improve accuracy. On the drug-sensitivity benchmark cohort, matched reference histories outperform swapped histories by an average of 13.0 percentage points in cluster-weighted accuracy. Decision-transition analysis separates corrections, newly introduced errors, and wrong-answer switches, revealing substantial answer changes hidden by small net accuracy differences. CellChain provides controlled comparisons for attributing changes in model predictions to prespecified expansions of biological context, including changes in evidence coverage, composition, and biological assignment.

title: GQL Datatypes as an RDF Vocabulary
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for DMKG 2026 (2nd International Workshop on Data Management for Knowledge Graphs), Bari, Italy
summary: The ISO GQL standard introduces a rich value-type system for property graphs, including scalar, temporal, byte-string, list, record, and dynamic union datatypes. The vocabulary presented here additionally covers a vector extension. At the same time, RDF-based knowledge graph systems identify literal datatypes by IRIs and interpret typed literals through value spaces, lexical spaces, and lexical-to-value mappings. This paper presents the GQL Datatypes RDF Vocabulary, a lightweight RDF vocabulary that represents selected GQL datatypes and the vector extension as RDF datatype IRIs and describes their hierarchy, aliases, and selected constraints using RDF, RDFS, OWL, and XML Schema Datatypes vocabulary terms. The vocabulary is intended to support interoperability between GQL-oriented property graph systems and RDF-based knowledge graph systems. We describe its namespace and datatype model, summarize its datatype coverage, and show how the accompanying generator and validator use the vocabulary. In the reference implementation, RDF literals retain GQL datatype IRIs; XSD mappings declared in the vocabulary support scalar validation, while lists, records, and vectors are encoded directly as JSON lexical forms of vocabulary-typed literals.

title: ML Engineering Agents - A Data Management Perspective
comment: 6 pages
summary: Machine learning engineering (MLE) agents are emerging as a new paradigm for automating end-to-end ML pipeline development. Using large language models for code generation and predictive performance as a machine-gradable feedback signal, these agents iteratively synthesize, execute, and refine pipeline code. Yet current systems are largely evaluated on pre-built, single-table benchmarks that abstract away key data management challenges. This tutorial introduces the foundations of MLE agents and highlights research opportunities for the database community. We cover how agents combine program synthesis with iterative and evolutionary optimization, and discuss open challenges in efficient pipeline execution, data discovery and augmentation over heterogeneous sources, reliability and debugging, as well as fairness and compliance. We connect these challenges to existing data management techniques and conclude with a hands-on session using contemporary MLE agents.

title: High-Throughput LLM-Based Compression and What It Takes: A Systems Study of Inference Engines and Entropy Coding Optimizations
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures. Published at ADMS 2026, co-located with VLDB 2026, Boston, USA
summary:
Large language models are attractive text compressors because next-token probabilities can be converted into code lengths. In practice, however, the main bottleneck is often not modeling quality but systems cost: a compressor must obtain logits quickly enough to compete with strong classical baselines.
  This paper examines systems optimizations for LLM-based compression, including multistream pipelined arithmetic coding and target-interval capture, and evaluates their trade-offs across inference engines, configurations and datasets. We evaluate LLM-based text compression on three different inference engines: Transformers, vLLM, and TensorRT-LLM. Notably, we obtain a speedup of 18.84x compared to prior work's Transformers implementation and a maximum recorded inference speed of 181 kilobytes per second at a compression ratio of 7.17, when running on an NVIDIA A100.

title: Path Length Existence Problems in Bounded-Treewidth Probabilistic Graphs
comment: 42 pages
summary:
We consider the problem of computing the probability of existence of a source-to-target path or walk satisfying a given length constraint in an input probabilistic graph. The length constraints we consider can require the length to be at least $\ell$, at most $\ell$, or exactly $\ell$, for $\ell$ a target length given as input. The probabilistic graphs that we consider are directed graphs where each edge is annotated with an independent probability of existence. As this task is generally intractable (#P-hard), we aim for algorithms applying to input graphs that are assumed to be of bounded treewidth. We classify the complexity landscape of these problems:
  - We give an XP algorithm parameterised by treewidth to compute the probability that an input probabilistic graph contains a source-to-target path/walk of length $\geq \ell$, and do the same for a path/walk of length $\leq \ell$.
  - We show that the four problems mentioned in the last item are W[1]-hard parameterised by pathwidth (hence not FPT under the standard assumption that FPT$\neq$W[1]). This is in contrast to the case of non-probabilistic graphs, where the corresponding problems were known to be FPT parameterised by treewidth; and to the connectivity problem (and more generally MSO evaluation) on probabilistic graphs, where the same was known.
  - Surprisingly, we show that it is #P-hard to compute the probability that an input graph contains a source-to-target path/walk of length exactly $\ell$, even on graphs of pathwidth $2$. By contrast, all our problems are tractable on graphs of treewidth $1$.
  - Last, we investigate the complexity of our problems when the edges can carry weights. This causes all our problems to become #P-hard already on pathwidth-2 graphs, and causes specifically the ``exactly $\ell$'' walk problem to be #P-hard even on pathwidth-1 graphs.

title: Query Optimization in the Wild: From Cross-platform Data Systems to Multi-agent Systems
summary: For decades the query optimizer has been the intellectual center of data management: the component that decides, on our behalf, how a declarative request should be executed. This talk traces a personal research path in which that same idea—separating what we want computed from how it is computed, and searching a large space of alternatives for a good plan—keeps resurfacing in new and larger guises. My journey passes through cross-platform data processing, where Apache Wayang made the execution engine the new unit of choice, moves on through the shift from hand-crafted to learned cost models and optimizers, and reaches today’s frontier: the optimization of multi-agent data pipelines, where the optimizer must jointly choose pipeline topology, language models, and execution engines under genuinely multi-objective, Pareto trade-offs. Along the way a new objective has become impossible to ignore: energy. Treating energy as a first-class optimization goal, alongside latency, monetary cost, and accuracy, is both a scientific opportunity for our community and a societal necessity.

title: The Case for Synthesized Data Compression
summary: Compression is a fundamental tool in data management. Today's compression schemes are generally designed by hand to apply to many different types of data (e.g., run length encoding or arithmetic encoding), leading to a zoo of general-purpose algorithms which work well for many datasets, but may not be optimal for any specific dataset. Inspired by recent advancements in agentic coding, we propose synthesizing custom-tailored data compression algorithms on a per-dataset basis. Unlike prior work using agents to synthesize database components, a data-specific compression algorithm can be fully verified at construction time, alleviating most correctness concerns. Modern file formats, like AnyBlox and F3, allow including the synthesized code alongside the data itself. Experimentally, we show that our synthesis agent can expand the compression-factor/decompression-speed Pareto front, outperforming general-purpose methods by nearly in compression factor.

title: Cache the Encoder Within: Compact, Reusable Memory across LLM Queries
summary: Repeated queries over shared documents incur redundant encoding, while caching model states introduces persistent storage costs. Building on CoMem's intermediate-state interface, EncBank treats a pretrained LLM's lower layers as a reusable document encoder and compactly stores their outputs for an adapted upper-layer reader. A self-distilled suffix adapter is shared across storage precisions within each backbone, without quantization-specific retraining. Across five benchmark suites on three Qwen backbones spanning different sizes and full-attention and hybrid architectures, 4-bit storage keeps each reported benchmark aggregate within one score point of native-precision EncBank. In a fixed Qwen3-8B workload, it retains 28.1% of the native-precision persistent GPU store. Separate native-precision controls yield a 1.40x selected-pack prefill speedup over same-evidence, same-adapter text replay, at a 3.12-point RULER accuracy cost. A native-precision Qwen3.8-27B configuration also passes 70 of 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks. EncBank thus combines reusable computation with compact memory, while task fidelity and end-to-end benefits remain dependent on the workload, preparation costs, and reuse frequency.

title: Preserving GPU Profiling Accuracy under Concurrent GPU-Coding Agent Workloads
summary: AI agents increasingly write and tune GPU code, but each optimization step needs an accurate profile from compiling and running candidate code on a GPU. Dedicated execution preserves accuracy but leaves GPUs mostly idle, whereas uncontrolled sharing improves utilization but corrupts the feedback that guides the agent’s search. This paper presents atomic profiling, which lets agents share a GPU server while making each measured interval dedicated-equivalent. PROFGUARD exploits the narrow waist of vendor timing and profiling APIs: it intercepts these APIs to find kernels and profiling operations that must run atomically, then coordinates CPU scheduling, GPU execution, and memory management so only protected intervals run with dedicated GPU access while other work continues to overlap. We implement PROFGUARD and evaluate it with a 1.5-hour replay of an agent trace. PROFGUARD keeps p95 CUPTI performance interference below 0.3%, reduces replay time by 3.9×, raises average GPU utilization from 15.1% to 58.7%, and eliminates the five unrecovered out-of-memory failures seen under uncontrolled concurrency.

title: Conversational Data Management: A Multi-agent Natural Language Interface for Semantic Data Lakes
summary: While modern data lakes offer powerful capabilities for handling heterogeneous datasets, interacting with them can be challenging, especially for users without technical expertise. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising solution: conversational access to complex data systems using plain language. This paper presents a novel natural language interface for semantic data lakes, designed to complement their existing user interface and lower the technical barrier for users. The system integrates LLMs into a modular, multi-agent architecture using retrieval-augmented generation and tool calling to decompose queries, plan workflows, and translate natural language into structured operations in the data lake. This enables seamless execution of tasks such as integration, discovery, and analytics without requiring users to understand system internals. We implemented the approach within our semantic data lake SEDAR, demonstrating its feasibility in a real data-centric environment. At the same time, the underlying multi-agent architecture is designed to be transferable and can be applied to other data-centric platforms. Evaluation on representative queries and multiple metrics shows that current LLMs can automate multi-step workflows, enhance accessibility, and robustly handle linguistic ambiguity. Our contribution is a reusable and system-independent agentic design pattern for helping to democratize data science for non-expert users.

title: Conflict hypergraphs for distinguishing feature selection: Structural limits and exact optimization
summary: Selecting Boolean features that preserve cross-class discernibility is a useful preprocessing objective for interpretable learning, yet pairwise graph abstractions can misrepresent the higher-arity constraint structure. Existing width arguments also leave unclear which hypergraph parameters actually make the Minimum Distinguishing Feature Set (MDFS) problem tractable. We formulate MDFS as hitting set, prove that it remains NP-hard even when hypertree width and fractional hypertree width equal one, and give exact dynamic programs parameterized either by join-boundary width or by decomposition width together with maximum hyperedge rank. Across six public datasets, MDFS compresses Mushroom from 117 to 5 features while attaining median rule-set AUC 0.988 and improves Titanic rule-set AUC from 0.785 for matched L1 selection to 0.799; across 60 optimization instances, a sampled GYO cyclic-residue measure correlates with CP-SAT runtime at Spearman .

title: Autonomous Database Administration Using Generative AI and Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Intelligent Enterprise Cloud Systems
summary: Enterprise database environments have grown into sprawling, heterogeneous estates spanning on-premises systems, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, Amazon Web Services, and Microsoft Azure, placing an unsustainable operational burden on human database administrators (DBAs). Traditional automation, rooted in rule-based monitoring and narrow machine learning models, addresses isolated tasks such as index tuning or anomaly scoring, but it cannot reason across the full administrative lifecycle, nor explain its decisions in terms a human operator can trust and act upon. This paper introduces the Artificial Intelligence Driven Autonomous Database Administration System (AIDAS), a novel conceptual framework that unifies generative artificial intelligence, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), vector search, multi-agent large language model (LLM) orchestration, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) into a single governed architecture for autonomous enterprise database administration. AIDAS is organized as a seven-layer pipeline spanning telemetry ingestion, enterprise knowledge retrieval, standardized tool access, multi-agent reasoning, governed execution, and continuous institutional-memory capture. Unlike prior LLM-for-database systems, which typically target a single task such as diagnosis or query rewriting, AIDAS is architected to intelligently automate monitoring, incident detection, root cause analysis, infrastructure troubleshooting, performance and query optimization, security monitoring, compliance validation, automated documentation, and decision support as a coherent whole, while remaining portable across heterogeneous cloud database platforms through an MCP-based integration fabric. The paper presents the system architecture, the enterprise RAG pipeline, the multi-agent decision workflow, a formal orchestration algorithm, an implementation strategy, and four enterprise use cases. Because AIDAS is presented as a design-science contribution rather than a deployed and empirically measured system, the performance discussion is framed conceptually against patterns reported in the cited AIOps and LLM-for-database literature, and empirical validation is explicitly identified as future work. Six original contributions are articulated and differentiated from existing enterprise AI database solutions, and the paper concludes with a candid discussion of limitations, including hallucination risk, MCP security exposure, and the governance requirements of autonomous change execution in production environments.

title: Learn Once, Evade Many: Hash-Center Task Construction for Universal NeuralHash Attacks
summary: Perceptual hash matching is an important client-side mechanism for detecting known harmful content in end-to-end encrypted systems, making the robustness of learned perceptual hashing increasingly critical. Existing NeuralHash attacks are predominantly input-specific and require a new optimization for each image. Universal perturbations avoid this repeated cost, but direct sample-wise optimization over facial identities can suffer from incompatible attack directions. We show that the key issue is how transferable tasks are constructed in NeuralHash's projected code space, rather than how sample gradients are merely aggregated. We therefore construct identity centers, sam pled sub-centers, and a global center to define local support and population-level query tasks; a lightweight first-order support query procedure only realizes this task decomposition. At τ = 17, the resulting reusable perturbation achieves a 100% attack success rate (ASR), 10 percentage points above the strongest compared universal baseline, with an LPIPS of 0.257. This work is a white-box robustness evaluation: after offline learning, the perturbation is reused on unseen identities without labels, center construction, or per-image gradient optimization.

title: LOOM: A Team-of-Agents Architecture for High-Performance Graph Analytics Workflows
summary: Teams of large language model (LLM) agents now plan, code, and verify their own work, yet nearly all agentic frameworks assume a dataset fits in the memory of one machine, excluding the billion-edge graphs that motivate high-performance computing and where a single poor analytical step can waste hours of supercomputer time. title: C-PAL: Design and Evaluation of a Cost-Aware Predictive Auto-Scaling Framework for AWS EC2
summary: Modern Cloud Applications have a trade off when it comes to the cost of their physical infrastructure versus the solidness of the service. Most of the current auto-scaling techniques provided by major cloud providers like AWS are mostly reactive. That means the scaling action is taken after a threshold is met. So instead of using an auto-scaling technique that reacts to a changing workload; C-PAL is a predictive costaware auto-scaling framework. The predictive engine uses a high precision long short-term memory (LSTM) algorithm to predict when workload surges will happen. Using this knowledge, C-PAL can proactively “pre-heat” resources before they are needed. Also, unlike most other auto-scaling techniques that scale using homogeneous scaling methods. C-PAL uses real time AWS pricing information to implement a heterogeneous resource mapping method. Therefore, C-PAL has the ability to choose between t3. medium, m5. large, and c5. large instances to provide the greatest cost benefit. The experimental results were obtained using high variance NASA HTTP traces. They showed that C-PAL was able to reduce the total operational cost of the system by 23.7%, while also increasing the overall reliability of the service by 75%. This was accomplished by reducing the Service Level Agreement (SLA) violation rate from 12% to 3%. Overall, these results confirm that both cost and reliability can be improved in cloud auto-scaling systems by utilizing the combination of deep learning-based workload predictions and cost effective architecture designs.

title: Stage-Wise Threshold Calibration for Early Defect Warning in Multi-Stage Manufacturing: A Cost-Sensitive Single-Line Automotive Case Study
summary: In multi-stage manufacturing, conformity is confirmed only at the final test, after the cost has been incurred. On an automotive assembly line (16,500 workpieces), a regression model per checkpoint predicts the final measurement; a threshold turns it into a Go/NoGo decision. On the holdout, the models ranked the defects (area under the curve, AUC, up to 0.81), yet at the inherited final-station limit they raised no alarm and missed all 15. The threshold was therefore calibrated per checkpoint on an earlier period under a cost-weighted objective with an explicit defect rate, and evaluated on a later holdout. Carried over as a value, it failed: 31% of production flagged during calibration became 89% on the holdout. Carried over as an alarm budget read off recent predictions and set from inspection capacity, it recovered 14 of 15 defects at a 36% false-alarm rate, below the cost of all nine baselines on this holdout; the cost objective at the defect rate the holdout later showed, a retrospective sensitivity scenario, gave the same count. Under 20 other seeds, the advantage over the closest rules did not hold, and a flag on the ramped-up variant, available beforehand, would have been cheaper. The evidence is a retrospective, single-line case study with 15 holdout defects; the rule is a candidate for shadow-mode evaluation, not a validated deployment policy.

title: ScoAI: Toward OR-Native Decision Intelligence
summary: Foundation models and AI agents are increasingly used to read operational requests, estimate uncertain quantities, and draft plans. In supply chains, these outputs feed decisions that must respect costs, stock and capacity limits, and business rules, and whose effects become visible only after delayed and often partial execution. This perspective, ScoAI= SC+ OR+ AI, argues that learned components should be designed around the decision they support. Supply-chain context defines the problem, operations research supplies objectives, constraints, and coordination, and AI supplies estimates and judgments that can be reused across tasks. We call a model or agent OR-native when these elements are explicit in its interface, and we refer to the coupling of learned components with executable operational relations as data--mechanism fusion. The coupling can fail in three places: when a judgment is turned into an action, when a locally good choice changes the cost of later stages, and when the executed action differs from the approved one. For each, we give a short analysis. Cost-sensitive thresholds and a decomposition of decision loss address the first; completion values and resource prices address the second; and a censoring argument shows how executed actions limit what operational logs can teach. Systems developed at JD. com illustrate these interfaces, and small constructed examples make every calculation reproducible. We close with decision records, an agent architecture, and evaluation protocols that compare reusable components with specialist workflows on decision quality, validity, coverage, and total cost.

title: Hallucination-Aware Hierarchical LLM for Autonomous UAV Mobility Control: A Safe Reinforcement Learning Approach
summary: This paper proposes SafeGPT, a hierarchical framework that integrates generative pretrained transformer (GPT)-based large language models (LLM) with safe reinforcement learning (safe-RL). SafeGPT addresses the large-scale random multi-point tour problem (RMPT) for multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). The target platforms are large electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) class rotary-wing UAVs. Such platforms suit wide-area logistics and infrastructure inspection rather than small drones. The hierarchical architecture enables scalable UAV coordination by centralizing strategic planning and distributing local route computation, mitigating the complexity issues of conventional methods. To mitigate LLM hallucination risks, ie, the generation of plausible routes that violate physical constraints, a safe-RL method is implemented as a constrained Markov decision process (MDP) with Lagrangian actor-critic optimization, which promotes constraints on energy consumption, communication efficiency, and duplicate visits. Comprehensive simulations demonstrate SafeGPT’s performance advantages in battery efficiency, communication reliability, and travel distance across problem scales from 500 to 2000 waypoints. Even in demanding scenarios, constraint violation rates remain below specified thresholds. These results establish SafeGPT as an effective solution for large-scale UAV route planning, respecting operational constraints without compromising efficiency.

title: Design of Collaborative Architecture for Android Mobile Smart Systems Based on Edge Computing
summary: Given the problems of limited computing resources, unstable network conditions, high cloud round-trip latency, and privacy risks in complex perception, real-time inference, and multimedia processing of Android mobile intelligent applications, this paper proposes an edge-cloud collaborative architecture. Add a task profiling, device state awareness and security caching module on the Android side, and set up service registration, dynamic scheduling, model caching and elastic resource pools at the edge. A multi-objective cost function is employed to optimise the ratio of task segmentation, edge node selection and computing resource allocation simultaneously. Monte Carlo simulations are carried out with publicly available reproducible parameters, and each data point is independently sampled 1200 times. Based on the above results, the proposed architecture can achieve an average response latency of 436.2 ms for a 6 MB task; this is a reduction of 60.3% and 59.0% compared with pure local execution and cloud execution, respectively, and reduces device-side power consumption by 84.1% over local execution. Therefore, the cooperative offloading of Android intelligent systems should not be based on a simple binary decision of" local or cloud", but should incorporate factors such as task granularity, link quality, device power consumption and edge load into a unified control loop.

title: Security Implications of Model Compression for Artificial Intelligence of Things Devices
summary: Consumer Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) devices are becoming increasingly prevalent in smart homes, wearables, healthcare products, and other consumer electronics. To enable deep learning inference on resource-constrained platforms, model compression techniques such as quantization and pruning are widely adopted to reduce memory usage, computation cost, latency, and energy consumption. However, these optimizations are not always security-neutral. Compression alters model parameters and internal representations, which may change its susceptibility to adversarial examples, backdoor attacks, membership inference, and deployment-stage tampering. This survey reviews the security implications of model compression, quantization, and pruning for consumer AIoT devices. We organize the literature through a modular analysis framework covering the data level, model level, and deployment level, and examine how compression interacts with robustness, privacy, integrity, availability, and deployment trust. We further summarize representative attack surfaces, evaluation metrics, mitigation strategies, and open challenges. This survey highlights the need to treat model compression not only as an efficiency optimization, but also as a security-relevant transformation in real-world AIoT deployment.

title: AI Large Model-Based Data Value Mining in Power Projects
summary: Power project usually has the characteristics of long construction period, many participants, complex supply chain and large number of project documents. Information such as schedule, earned value, cost, contract changes, quality, safety, equipment delivery, BIM/IoT, and meeting records are usually stored in separate systems. Therefore, although the data are available, they may not provide timely decision support for project management. Traditional statistical models are not good at interpreting narrative evidence. When the project conditions or supply conditions change, the prediction accuracy of the static model may also decrease. In order to solve these problems, this paper proposes Power-LLM ValueLoop, a closed-loop framework for data value mining supported by large models. The framework identifies entities, events, causal signals, urgency, conflict evidence, and confidence levels through a pattern-based large model layer, and associates relevant results with structured data such as schedule, cost, resources, quality, and supply chain. Subsequently, the semantic-time model is used to estimate and calibrate the probability of major delays or failure events in the next 4 weeks. Confirmed outcomes, human corrections, time-decayed learning, drift monitoring, and threshold adjustment form the feedback loop. The system can deliver traceable risk early warnings, identify key risk drivers, and provide action recommendations for review by project personnel. This paper uses a synthetic project portfolio for evaluation, including 720 power engineering projects, 10 start-up batches, and 15,653 project-week observation records. Controlled concept drift was introduced from the 6th batch. In the four batches after drift, the macro average ROC-AUC of the feedback model was 0.773, the macro average PR-AUC was 0.366, and the Brier score was 0.105. At the recall-oriented operating point, the model identified 78.1% of the risks in the next four weeks, with an average warning advance of about 9.1 weeks. For 80.2% of the event items, the system can issue an early warning at least 4 weeks before the event. Compared with the static AI fusion model, the feedback mechanism improves the recall rate by about 0.140, but the false alarm rate also increases from 0.275 to 0.391. This shows that the improvement of model performance still needs to rely on reasonable threshold management and manual review. A supplementary Monte Carlo decision analysis examines prevalence and error-cost sensitivity at fixed operating rates. At the reported test prevalence, feedback has lower expected error loss only when the missed-event cost exceeds approximately 5.35 times the false-alarm cost. This conditional result does not establish savings in deployed projects.

title: AI-Driven Natural Resource Optimization and Financial Performance in the Automotive Industry: A PRISMA-Based Systematic Review of Twelve Artificial Intelligence …
summary: The global automobile sector generates more than USD 2.8 trillion in annual revenue and employs over 8 million people, making it one of the most capital-intensive and operationally complex industries in the world economy, with multi-tiered supply chains spanning dozens of countries. Amid the parallel transformations of electrification, digitalisation and tightening environmental regulation, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a primary enabler of financial performance across the automotive value chain. This systematic review synthesises the application of twelve AI-technique families like supervised machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, reinforcement learning, mixed-integer linear programming (MILP), time-series econometrics, computer vision, simulation and digital twins, structural/causal inference, graph and network AI, hybrid ensembles, and federated learning to automotive financial decision-making. Following PRISMA 2025 guidelines, 4,217 records were retrieved from five major databases (2012–2025), yielding 128 eligible studies after multi-stage screening and CASP-based quality appraisal, of which five landmark studies were subjected to extended critical appraisal. We cross-tabulate the twelve AI-technique families against eight financial-performance dimensions are cash-flow optimisation, cost reduction, revenue and pricing, market stability, innovation return on investment, working-capital efficiency, quality/warranty cost, and ESG compliance. The synthesised evidence shows that MILP-based production scheduling reduces late-invoiced orders by up to 76% and inventory holding costs by 20.4%; reinforcement-learning-based dynamic pricing raises revenue by 8-12%; and computer-vision-based quality inspection reduces warranty cost exposure by USD 50-200 million per OEM per year. These gains are, however, materially conditioned by data quality, implementation context, and organisational maturity. The review further identifies ten priority research gaps are most urgently, causal identification, real-time closed-loop AI-financial integration, and explainability under emerging regulatory regimes that define an academic and industrial research agenda for the coming decade.

title: QoS-Aware Choreography in the Internet of Things Based on Forecast-Guided Binding and Local Rebinding
summary: Internet of Things (IoT) service choreographies integrate services across devices, edge servers and the cloud without a central orchestrator. Existing quality-of-service (QoS)-aware composition methods use single-value QoS, separable objectives and one-shot binding, overlooking evolving service conditions, peer-link dependencies and rebinding costs. This paper proposes MDP-BWO, a Markov decision process (MDP)-guided Black Widow Optimization (BWO) framework that integrates state forecasting, dependency-aware binding and runtime adaptation. A three-state Markov chain learned from monitoring traces forecasts each service’s state occupancy and guides BWO over constrained, non-separable bindings; each participant rebinds locally by table lookup of a finite-horizon MDP policy over a value-selected shortlist. In simulations on synthetic and WS-DREAM-based instances (measured QoS, synthetic state dynamics; 14 configurations × 30 held-out seeds), MDP-BWO outperforms six baselines with reactive fail-over in every configuration, raising executed utility by 0.086–0.139 and the solved-request rate by 0.087–0.130 (Holm-corrected p < 0.05); latency on WS-DREAM and cost on synthetic instances do not improve over three of the population baselines. Most of the gain comes from MDP rebinding; with the same forecast and policy, MDP-BWO still outperforms five population-based searches in 11–14 configurations and is matched or slightly exceeded only by an exact mixed-integer search with 14–43 times longer mean planning time.
